paragraphs.heading: A number whose square is −1
paragraphs.text: The imaginary unit, usually written i, is a constant that solves the equation x² = −1, which no real number can solve. In fact i is defined by that single property: i² = −1. Any real number multiplied by i is called an imaginary number.

paragraphs.heading: Building the complex numbers
paragraphs.text: Combine the real numbers with i using addition and multiplication, and you get a new number system called the complex numbers. Each of them has the form a + bi, where a and b are real. To calculate with them, treat i as an unknown letter and replace every i² with −1. In this form, i itself is 0 + 1i, with a real part of zero and an imaginary part of one.

paragraphs.heading: Two roots that look alike
paragraphs.text: The number −1 has two different square roots, i and −i. Likewise, every nonzero complex number has two square roots, each the negative of the other, while zero has only zero. Strangely, i and −i cannot be told apart by their properties: nothing is true of one that is not true of the other. Which one is called +i is just a label, and despite their signs neither is positive or negative the way real numbers are.

paragraphs.heading: Where i sits on the plane
paragraphs.text: In the complex plane, real numbers run along the horizontal axis and imaginary numbers along the vertical one. There i is the point one unit from the origin on the imaginary axis, the same distance from 0 as 1 but at a right angle to it. In polar form it is e^(πi/2), with a size of 1 and an angle of π/2 radians. Adding a complex number shifts the plane, and multiplying by one of size 1 rotates it about the origin.

paragraphs.heading: Why imaginary
paragraphs.text: In early-modern mathematics, only what we now call real numbers, the ones you get from measuring or simple arithmetic, counted as numbers at all. Even negative numbers were met with doubt, so a square root of a negative number seemed meaningless, and such roots were called imaginary. The name is generally credited to René Descartes, and Isaac Newton was using it by 1670. Leonhard Euler introduced the letter i. Whatever the name suggests, the idea is mathematically sound.

paragraphs.heading: Other ways to write it
paragraphs.text: In the past the imaginary unit was written √(−1), though that is now rare. Where the letter i would cause confusion, j is sometimes used instead. Electrical engineers, for example, normally write j, because i usually stands for electric current.
